line: Each word gets its label from the typeset source, which serves as the ground truth.
The scorer compares every block with the ground truth.
We treat the labels of the LaTeX source as ground truth.
The rules of one block are the baseline against which the region rule is measured.
Condition A, today's request, is the baseline.
Against this baseline the memory moves the probes from 15.1% to 55.6%.
An ablation of the region rule shows what it adds to the rules of one block.
In the ablation study we remove one rule at a time and score the held-out set again.
Each ablation changes exactly one rule.
The constants were fitted on the development set.
Papers and cases each have a development set and a held-out set.
Recall on the development set rises from 0.56 to 0.91.
The held-out set was not used to choose any constant.
On the held-out set the region rule changes nothing.
The result on the held-out set is the one we report.
Recall is low because the reader garbles formulas before the rule sees them.
Adding the region rule raises recall from 0.78 to 1.00.
The one-block rules reach a recall of 0.59 on the paper.
Precision stays at 1.00 while recall rises.
The precision of the rule is 0.90 on the held-out paper.
We report precision and recall for the keep decision.
The rules keep 26 of 44 true blocks at three false positives.
A false positive leaves a sentence untranslated.
The region rule produced one false positive on the cases.
The oracle that replays the references gives an upper bound of 312 of 312.
This score is an upper bound, not a result.
The oracle sets the upper bound for every condition.
A sign test on the probes where the two runs disagree gives p < 0.0001.
We use a sign test because the probes are paired.
The sign test is computed over the discordant probes only.
The controls are probes that any engine should get right.
The memory leaves the controls unchanged.
On the controls the two conditions are within noise.
On a cold start the document reader compiles its model, which can take tens of seconds.
After a cold start the first read is slow.
A cold start of the service is the worst case for the first line.
With a warm cache the same read answers in a fraction of a second.
Once the compile cache is warm, the reader answers at once.
A warm cache removes the compile from the path.
We do not report a cache hit rate, because no committed result measures it.
The cache hit rate of a scroll through a feed depends on how many lines repeat.
A higher cache hit rate means fewer requests to the engine.
The throughput of the capture path is bounded by the frame interval.
Batching three lines raises the throughput of the engine.
We measure throughput in lines per second.
The committed results give medians and say nothing about the tail latency.
Tail latency matters more than the median for a lens over a scroll.
The tail latency of the document reader is set by its cold start.
The service is put to rest with an exponential back-off of 1, 2, 4 up to 30 s.
The back-off keeps a slow reader from being asked again at once.
After each late answer the back-off doubles.
Fitting constants on the development set risks overfitting.
The held-out set guards against overfitting.
Overfitting would show as a gap between the two sets.
Differences under about 0.3 are noise.
A second run of A gives the noise floor of the bench.
The change is within the noise.
With 312 probes the confidence interval is about plus or minus five points.
We report no confidence interval for the engine bench.
The confidence interval of the difference excludes zero.
Calibration items that are the same text twice must come back as ties.
The judge passes the calibration when it ties identical texts.
We run a calibration before every judging round.
The warm median of a batch of three lines is 0.15 s.
We report the median over twelve lines.
The median hides the slowest batches.
A regression in the scroll predictor shows as drift.
The gate fails on any regression of the held-out score.
We check each change for regressions.
